prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

the neighbourhood. Even repeated experience of bumping into people, or greeting each other on the street will help people feel connected to other people and the places. In this sense, walkability can be seen as an important aspect for building a better community. Jane Jacobs (1961) in her influential work, The Death and Life of Great American Cities suggested to rethink the single use, car oriented modernist way of planning (Jacobs, 1961). Groups such as New Urbanists supported this idea and promoted mixed-use and walkable neighbourhood (Christopher B. Leinberger, 2009). Scholars such as Jan Gehl have done multiple study on street life and emphasized the importance of human scale and social activities between buildings (cid:19)(cid:2)(cid:7)(cid:9)(cid:10)(cid:1)(cid:5)(cid:12)(cid:6)(cid:1)(cid:2)(cid:7)(cid:11)(cid:16)ø(cid:7)(cid:17)(cid:1)(cid:23)(cid:21)(cid:21)(cid:24)(cid:18)(cid:1)(cid:2)(cid:7)(cid:9)(cid:10)(cid:1)(cid:5)(cid:12)(cid:6)(cid:1)(cid:4)(cid:13)(cid:8)(cid:7)(cid:14)(cid:15)(cid:17)(cid:1)(cid:23)(cid:21)(cid:22)(cid:21)(cid:18)(cid:1)(cid:3)(cid:5)(cid:12)(cid:1)(cid:2)(cid:7)(cid:9)(cid:10)(cid:17)(cid:1)(cid:23)(cid:21)(cid:22)(cid:22)(cid:20). Mixed use and walkable streets are inherent features of old cities, including those in Japan, many parts of which were lost during the modern development. In historical city centres like that of Kyoto, the changes have been gradual compared to other large cities, but many developments have taken place along wider streets and walkable areas in Kyoto are now fragmented. 2. Structure of Historical Japanese Cities and Problems Related to Pedestrian Safety Traditional Japanese cities are structured according to a strict grid system. The old city plans typically do not include public squares or large open spaces (Jinnai, 1995). The size of each grid is relatively large, for example, in the case of Kyoto the grid was approximately 120 x 120m. This was too large for individual buildings. Therefore, smaller streets and alleyways developed rather irregularly to provide access to the inner plots. It can be said that public open spaces in the traditional Japanese neighbourhoods are structured only with streets. Therefore, the separation between human and wheeled traffic becomes fundamental. However, since the 1950s, the spread of cars have become more and more evident throughout Japan. Wider streets became populated with cars. This was further accelerated by Japan’s economic growth from 1960 to 1970s, where wider roads were much needed for transports of goods and people. As a result, the flow of pedestrians were often de-prioritised in the modern street design in Japan. According to the Building Standards Act amended in 1950, minimum width of a road is determined as 4 metres (I will call this the 4-metre rule), which is the width that two cars can barely pass by each other. When a road is built fulfilling the minimum requirement, there is not enough space left for the pedestrians. As a result, many roads in urban areas of Japan are built with little to no pedestrian facilities. Some have very narrow sidewalks, and others have only white lines separating the pedestrian space from the rest of the road. According to several sources of municipalities, they consider it important to keep the width of the road wide enough so that emergency vehicles can go through in case of disaster (Narita City, 2010; The City of Suzuka, 2014). This is reasonable as when the Great Hanshin Awaji earthquake happened in 1995, it was reported that ambulances and fire engines could not go through the densely built areas

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

Mixed use and walkable streets are inherent features of old cities, including those in Japan, many parts of which were lost during the modern development. In historical city centres like that of Kyoto, the changes have been gradual compared to other large cities, but many developments have taken place along wider streets and walkable areas in Kyoto are now fragmented. 2. Structure of Historical Japanese Cities and Problems Related to Pedestrian Safety Traditional Japanese cities are structured according to a strict grid system. The old city plans typically do not include public squares or large open spaces (Jinnai, 1995). The size of each grid is relatively large, for example, in the case of Kyoto the grid was approximately 120 x 120m. This was too large for individual buildings. Therefore, smaller streets and alleyways developed rather irregularly to provide access to the inner plots. It can be said that public open spaces in the traditional Japanese neighbourhoods are structured only with streets. Therefore, the separation between human and wheeled traffic becomes fundamental. However, since the 1950s, the spread of cars have become more and more evident throughout Japan. Wider streets became populated with cars. This was further accelerated by Japan’s economic growth from 1960 to 1970s, where wider roads were much needed for transports of goods and people. As a result, the flow of pedestrians were often de-prioritised in the modern street design in Japan. According to the Building Standards Act amended in 1950, minimum width of a road is determined as 4 metres (I will call this the 4-metre rule), which is the width that two cars can barely pass by each other. When a road is built fulfilling the minimum requirement, there is not enough space left for the pedestrians. As a result, many roads in urban areas of Japan are built with little to no pedestrian facilities. Some have very narrow sidewalks, and others have only white lines separating the pedestrian space from the rest of the road. According to several sources of municipalities, they consider it important to keep the width of the road wide enough so that emergency vehicles can go through in case of disaster (Narita City, 2010; The City of Suzuka, 2014).
